items.title: English has no official regulator
items.claim: French has the Académie française, Spanish has the Real Academia. What regulates English?

options.text: The Oxford English Dictionary serves as the official standard
Nothing — there is no official body. English is regulated descriptively by usage, with dictionaries and style guides documenting (not dictating) it
The Royal Society of English, founded by Charles II
The British Council, in coordination with the US State Department

items.reveal:
Jonathan Swift proposed an English Academy in 1712 ('A Proposal for Correcting, Improving and Ascertaining the English Tongue'). It was never founded. Samuel Johnson, when compiling his 1755 Dictionary, ridiculed the idea — by the time he finished, his early prescriptivism had given way to acceptance that language changes.

The OED, Merriam-Webster and others are descriptive references. Style guides (Fowler, Chicago, AP) influence but do not legislate. This 'distributed' status is one reason English absorbs loanwords and tolerates variation so readily.
items.why: Students often assume 'correct English' is a fixed object enforced from above. It isn't. Norms emerge from publication, prestige and use — a system, not a rulebook.

items.title: African American Vernacular English has its own grammar
items.claim: AAVE features like 'He be working' are often treated as 'bad grammar'. What is the linguistic reality?

options.text: AAVE is broken English with no consistent grammatical rules
AAVE has systematic grammar including a 'habitual be' that marks repeated action — a tense distinction Standard English cannot make as economically
AAVE is identical to Standard English with different vocabulary
AAVE is a recent invention from hip-hop culture

items.reveal:
'He working' means he is working right now. 'He be working' means he works habitually or regularly. Standard English cannot mark this distinction without adverbs ('he usually works').

William Labov's 1970s work, and subsequent scholarship by John Rickford, Geneva Smitherman and others, documented AAVE's consistent rules: copula deletion in specific syntactic environments, the habitual 'be', stressed 'BIN' marking remote past ('He BIN finished').

The 1996 Oakland Ebonics controversy hinged on this — linguists supported recognising AAVE as a rule-governed variety; politicians and pundits largely did not.
items.why: 'Bad English' is almost always a sociological judgment, not a linguistic one. Linguists describe what speakers actually do; AAVE does sophisticated work Standard English doesn't.

items.title: English pronunciation changed completely between Chaucer and Shakespeare
items.claim: Why does 'name' rhyme with 'fame' (long /eɪ/) when in Chaucer's time it was pronounced 'nah-meh'?

options.text: A gradual French influence after the Norman Conquest
The Great Vowel Shift — a chain reaction in which long vowels raised and diphthongised across English, roughly 1400-1700
Shakespeare deliberately reformed English pronunciation for his plays
The printing press standardised pronunciation by reading instructions in books

items.reveal_title: A chain reaction in the mouth
items.reveal:
Otto Jespersen named the Great Vowel Shift in 1909. Middle English long /aː/ ('ah') raised to /eː/, /eː/ to /iː/, and high vowels /iː/ and /uː/ diphthongised to /aɪ/ and /aʊ/.

This is why English spelling matches pre-shift pronunciation but mouths don't: 'name' was 'nahme', 'meet' was 'mate', 'time' was 'teem', 'house' was 'hoose'. Caxton's printing press (1476) froze spelling roughly mid-shift, leaving the mismatch we live with.

Causes are debated: post-plague demographic mixing, social pressure from emerging middle-class speech, internal phonological pressure.
items.why: English spelling looks broken because it preserves the pronunciation of a language nobody alive speaks. The shift is also why Chaucer is hard to read aloud — you're not just decoding spelling, you're hearing a different sound system.
